#!/bin/bash
# build one C# file the way the lessons do: inside the image's restored project
set -e
rm -rf /tmp/cs && cp -r /opt/templates/csharp /tmp/cs && cp "$1" /tmp/cs/Program.cs
cd /tmp/cs && dotnet build --no-restore -v q -nologo -clp:NoSummary
dotnet bin/Debug/net10.0/Program.dll

gotcha.title: Using `?` on an error your function can't hold
gotcha.looks_fine: `fs::read_to_string(path)?` reads like the usual "pass the error up" step, so it seems the function can simply let the `io::Error` out.
gotcha.rust_sees: This function promises to return a `ConfigError`. `fs::read_to_string` fails with an `io::Error`, and Rust doesn't know how to turn one into the other.
gotcha.why: `?` can convert errors, but only along a route you've written: an `impl From<io::Error> for ConfigError`, or a `#[from]` on a variant with thiserror. Or convert by hand with `map_err`, as the fix below and the program on this page do. A function that returns `anyhow::Result` accepts any error that implements `std::error::Error` (and is `Send + Sync + 'static`), so it needs no conversion.

fixed.name: src/main.rs

go.says: Go compiles and runs this. The function returns the `error` interface, which any error value satisfies, so `return "", err` type-checks.
go.out: open missing.conf: no such file or directory

kotlin.says: Kotlin compiles and runs this, and the exception is caught as `IOException`. A thrown exception travels up the stack, and the signature does not name its type. So there is nothing to convert, and no rule to break.

java.says: Java refuses a version of this too: a method that declares `throws ConfigError` cannot let an `IOException` escape, and `javac` says `unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown`. Java's rule is about checked exceptions; Rust's is about the `Result` type.

csharp.says: Not run here. C# has no checked exceptions: a method does not declare the exceptions it throws.

c.says: Not run here. A C function reports failure through its return value or `errno`, and nothing converts one kind of error into another for you.

cpp.says: Not run here. A C++ function can throw an exception of any type; its signature does not list them.
